texts: good. the definite plural becomes a group of copper cauldrons and "old" is handed to each cauldron by a fireable rule, rather than predicated of the group as a thing.
good. the family, its location in Faltern, the forging event, the cauldrons and the past tense are all covered.
good. the inability is recorded as one denied bundle covering the whole "can replace a lost cauldron" claim, with the village typed outside the denial.

bad: a possessive cannot ride a kind-level claim in our instruction set, so "a Keeper's" is either pinned on one particular anonymous Keeper (as here, which wrongly makes that one Keeper the owner of the entire brass-snuffer kind) or dropped altogether. Split the ownership into its own clause: "A brass snuffer is a tool. Every Keeper owns a personal brass snuffer." - the universal then gives each Keeper their own snuffer, and nothing about the tool or its being personal is lost.

mixed: faithful as written, but "A Keeper" mints one anonymous Keeper, so the parse records that one individual's habit rather than a practice of Keepers generally - no other Keeper inherits it. If you mean the standing practice, write "Keepers extinguish the lantern at dawn with a brass snuffer."; a bare plural is what turns the sentence into a rule reaching every Keeper.

bad: two things go wrong. "A Keeper" again names one anonymous Keeper rather than Keepers in general, and on the strict reading that also strands "often", which has no carrier outside a rule about a kind; and "with the station" is recorded as a second direct object of "inherits" instead of an accompanying thing. A bare plural fixes the first half: "Keepers often inherit the snuffer with the station." - that licenses the "often" reading over every Keeper; the double-object slip is ours to fix.

mixed: the useful content is there - a wick-trimmer is a tool, is personal, and trims wicks - but the possessive lands as a kind-to-kind link (the wick-trimmer kind belongs to the Keeper kind), which does not say that each trimmer is some particular Keeper's, and the identically shaped brass-snuffer sentence in this item parsed a different way again. Same fix as there: "A wick-trimmer is a tool. Every Keeper owns a personal wick-trimmer."
